title: Why green wood works
subtitle: The science behind the freshly-cut state
excerpt: Green wood is not just unseasoned wood. Its cellular structure is actively different from seasoned wood: the cell walls are saturated and the fibres flex rather than crack. This article explains the moisture gradient, why that makes hand tools effective, and what changes as the wood dries.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily under hand tools.
The weight of water in a piece of wood expressed as a percentage of the dry weight of the wood.

content.text: Green wood is freshly felled or recently riven wood with a

above the fibre saturation point, which is typically 25 to 30 per cent for most British hardwoods. The cells of the wood still contain free water in the cell lumens and bound water in the cell walls. That bound water plasticises the lignin that holds the cell walls rigid, which is why
carves and shaves with much less force than seasoned wood.
What changes as the wood dries

As moisture leaves the wood, the cell walls shrink and the lignin hardens. The wood becomes dimensionally smaller (this is why green wood joints shrink and tighten) and mechanically harder. The shrinkage is not uniform: the wood shrinks much more across the grain (tangentially and radially) than along it (longitudinally). This uneven shrinkage causes most of the problems with drying wood: cupping, checking, and warping all come from the differential shrinkage across different zones of the cross-section.
Why a drawknife works better in green wood

In seasoned wood, the cell walls have stiffened and the knife must deform them to cut. More force is needed and the cutting edge dulls faster. In green wood, the plasticised cell walls flex ahead of the blade and separate more cleanly. The same edge removes a given volume of material in roughly half the strokes compared to seasoned equivalent. This is the practical reason green woodworkers prefer fresh material and why the tools feel completely different from bench-woodworking.

Green wood does not stay green indefinitely after felling. The outer zone (the sapwood) loses moisture fastest; the inner zone (heartwood) more slowly. For most British hardwoods, the working window at which the wood is still easy to shave but not yet starting to check is two to six weeks after felling, depending on the season and storage. In summer the window is shorter; in winter, when evaporation is slower, it extends to six weeks or more. Keep green material in a shaded, ventilated space rather than in a sealed bag or directly on concrete, which holds moisture unevenly.

One important technique in green woodwork is the deliberate mismatch of moisture content in a joint. A green tenon fitted into a seasoned mortise will shrink as it dries, loosening the joint. A seasoned tenon fitted into a green mortise will be gripped tighter as the mortise shrinks around it: a self-locking joint with no glue. This is how traditional Welsh and Winsor chair legs are fitted. The leg tenon is slightly oversize when fitted green; as the seat board dries around it, the joint tightens and becomes effectively permanent.
Species differences in the green state
Ash: easy to rive, easy to shave. Dries straight. The best all-round green-woodwork species in Britain.
Hazel: very easy to work green. Slightly softer than ash and dries quickly. The right species for baskets, hurdles, and walking sticks.
Oak: rives well along the rays in the green state. Harder to carve than ash green, and the tannins in oak stain iron tools. Clean tools after use on green oak.
Sycamore: carves well green. Slightly more likely to check on the end grain than ash; keep end grain sealed with wax or PVA while drying if the piece has exposed end grain.
